digest.intro: Arms races, institutional sabotage, and a fly that escapes with real neurons.

items.title: Ukrainian Drones Overwhelm Russian Tanks' New Active Protection System — For Now
items.blurb: Russia's Arena-M active protection system made its combat debut on July 22 in Donetsk and did manage to shoot down incoming drones — but Ukrainian operators responded by saturating each tank with 15–20 drones until it died anyway. The telling detail is the arithmetic: defense works until it doesn't scale, and the defenders are already iterating on the ratio. Rob Lee's read is that this isn't a failure story, it's the opening move of a new layer in the arms race.

items.title: The United States Is About to Wake Up to the Threat from China's Space Program
items.blurb: Chang'e 7 is launching as soon as this Sunday — China's most sophisticated lunar mission yet, targeting the south pole — and the geopolitical stakes aren't really about who plants a flag first. The argument being made seriously now is that a Chinese lunar landing before NASA's return resets the century's superpower narrative in ways Apollo's legacy can't insulate against. The shared-commons assumption about space is quietly evaporating.

items.title: Disney Sues FCC and Its Chair, Escalating Fight Against Trump's Chief Censor
items.blurb: Disney, ABC, and eight broadcast stations filed a First Amendment lawsuit against the FCC and Chair Brendan Carr, seeking a temporary restraining order to halt license renewal proceedings that Disney calls direct retaliation for ABC's editorial choices. The specific mechanism matters: a Hearing Designation Order, if issued, would all but guarantee license loss — making this a test of whether the executive branch can use regulatory process as a speech weapon. This is structural, not a PR dispute.

items.title: A 3D Fruit Fly on macOS Desktop Powered by the Real FlyWire Connectome
items.blurb: Someone took the complete FlyWire connectome — 139,255 neurons mapped — extracted a 668-neuron escape circuit with ~19,000 real synaptic connections, ran it as a 1kHz leaky-integrate-and-fire simulation, and made it a desktop pet. When you move your cursor fast toward it, the Giant Fiber neurons actually spike through real synaptic pathways and the fly bolts in ~4ms, exactly as a biological fly does; slow approaches are tolerated because 1,200 feedforward inhibition synapses push back. This is a real biological system rendered as interactive geometry, and it's free to run.

items.title: Robin Sloan: Dragoncatcher — Jarvising
items.blurb: Sloan notices that the most common use of a personal AI agent is... refining the personal AI agent. 'Gotta get my tools just right' has always been a way to avoid making the thing. His corrective is a scene from TNG where Geordi uses the ship's Computer and holodeck together to actually solve a mystery — anonymous, powerful, collaborative — which he argues is a richer model than the flattering Jarvis/Tony Stark fantasy. Short, sharp, and worth two minutes if you've been tinkering more than making lately.

items.title: Finger: The 1971 Social Network That Never Died
items.blurb: Finger was born at Stanford's AI Lab in 1971 because Les Earnest kept watching researchers run their fingers down a WHO display trying to find colleagues — so he built a protocol that let you query a plain text file about any user on any connected machine. John Carmack used it as a public dev journal during the Quake era; it still works today; your Mac has the client installed. The piece is a genuinely good archaeology of how presence, identity, and social norms on networks were shaped by a tool almost no one knows existed.

items.title: Julie Green's 'The Last Supper' Memorializes Hundreds of People's Final Meals While on Death Row
items.blurb: From 1999 until her death in 2021, Green painted final meal requests from death row inmates in cobalt blue mineral paint on mass-produced ceramic platters — everything from KFC buckets to a single plate reading 'NONE.' One plate reads 'He never had a birthday cake, so we ordered a birthday cake for him. He was only 15.' Green's own line — 'Selections provide clues on region, race, and economic background' — is the whole project in a sentence: the most ordinary human act, choice of food, as the last legible trace of a person the system otherwise renders invisible.

items.title: Sipho Mabona: Milk Cartons and Bottle Gourds Form a Tribute to His Late Father
items.blurb: Mabona cut triangular and rectangular windows into dried calabash gourds and replaced them with fragments of Tetra Pak milk cartons — the same material that displaced the calabash as a beverage container — stitched with colored thread, each piece centered on a small curved mirror. Embedded audio plays his late father, scholar and activist Mongameli Mabona, reading his own poems and his doctoral thesis on Xhosa cultural history. The swap of materials isn't metaphor bolted on; it's structural: the thing that replaced the thing, made to carry the memory of what it replaced.

items.title: Thieves of Cursed Rocks Pen Letters of Remorse to a National Park
items.blurb: Petrified Forest National Park receives a steady stream of stolen rocks mailed back by visitors convinced the theft cursed their lives — car accidents, divorces, job losses, mysterious illness. Aeon's documentary short treats these letters as genuine folk mythology: secular people, confronted with bad luck, reaching for magical causality and choosing confession as the remedy. It's guilt archaeology, and it says something true about how thin the rationalist layer actually is.

facts.fact: Ukrainian soldiers reported needing 15–20 kamikaze drones to destroy each Russian tank equipped with the Arena-M active protection system, because the system successfully intercepted some incoming drones during its July 22 combat debut.

The desktop fruit fly simulation runs a 668-neuron circuit with ~19,000 real synaptic connections at 1kHz, and its escape response triggers in ~4ms — the same latency as a biological fly — because the Giant Fiber neurons must genuinely spike through real connectome pathways, not a scripted animation.

Narwhal tusks contain not one but two nested spirals oriented in opposite directions — a left-handed outer spiral and a right-handed internal one — a structure only revealed by X-ray imaging and reported in Nature Communications.

The Trump administration has cut AHRQ staff by 75 percent, canceled over 100 grants worth more than $250 million, and is declining to spend most of the $345 million Congress appropriated for the agency in 2026 — with only $15 million disbursed in grants so far.

Finger, the 1971 social networking protocol that lets you query a plain text file about any user on a connected machine, is still operational today and comes pre-installed as a client on macOS and most Unix systems.

art_picks.title: Sans Soleil
art_picks.creator: Chris Marker
art_picks.why: A film that functions as a philosophical essay on memory, ritual, and how images construct time — Marker drifts between Japan, Guinea-Bissau, and Iceland, finding feedback loops between culture and self-mythology. Nothing else puts the invisible architecture of everyday life on screen like this.

art_picks.title: Cybernetic Serendipity (1968 exhibition documentation)
art_picks.creator: Jasia Reichardt / ICA London
art_picks.why: The founding moment where art, systems thinking, and computation collided in public — a frontier scene still forming its own rules, where code was expression and machines made poetry. The documentation reads as a time capsule of a world figuring out what software-as-self-expression even means.

art_picks.title: Tri Repetae
art_picks.creator: Autechre
art_picks.why: Pure expressive systems — generative industrial textures that feel both deeply inhuman and emotionally precise. The 1995 landmark where machine logic becomes its own aesthetic grammar; still the clearest proof that technical constraint can produce something that feels like breath.

events.name: André Masson: Bodies, Cities, Kingdoms — Drawings from Automatism to Metamorphosis, 1924–1941
events.why: Masson's automatist drawings are the raw wiring beneath Surrealism — unconscious systems made visible on paper, where bodies dissolve into landscapes and back; a quietly radical body of work that still looks like nothing else.

events.name: Marcel Duchamp Retrospective — Final Days
events.venue: Museum of Modern Art (MoMA), 11 W 53rd St, Manhattan
events.why: The first major North American Duchamp survey in 50+ years — nearly 300 works spanning readymades, film, painting, and the unclassifiable — closes Saturday; the man who broke the boundary between art and idea, and whose revolutions still quietly run the contemporary art world.

events.name: Whitney Biennial 2026 — Final Days
events.venue: Whitney Museum of American Art, 99 Gansevoort St, Manhattan
events.why: The 82nd edition closes Sunday — one of the few recurring exhibitions that functions as a live index of where American art is actually going, not where institutions wish it would; worth a final pass before it disappears.

events.name: Devon Turnbull — HiFi Pursuit Listening Room Dream No. 3
events.venue: Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum, 2 E 91st St, Manhattan
events.why: Turnbull has converted the Carnegie Mansion's historic library into a hand-built 'shrine to music' — large-scale sculptural audio equipment designed to slow you down and make listening a physical, spatial act; exactly the kind of obsessive craft-meets-space work that makes you want to go build something.

events.name: Verve Records 70th Anniversary — Samara Joy & Christian McBride / Mei Semones plays Getz/Gilberto
events.why: Free, outdoor, late-evening celebration of one of jazz's most mythologized labels — Samara Joy and McBride on the catalog, plus a full Getz/Gilberto live set and a DJ closing; a ritual performance of a recording that itself became a cultural symbol.
